Q: Use mod_rewrite to create custom directory index in Apache A:

Why do you think Apache Directory listings "suck"?

It has a LOT of features, such as user controllable headers, footers, icon based on file type, descriptions of specific files, automatically ignores files that are denied access, can specify files to ignore in the listing but which remain accessible, etc., etc., etc..

I'd love to have the Apache directory listing generated extracted from Apache to use outside of Apache, as I have not found a directory listing program that matches it. So may index generators are just so overly complicated (developed from complex templating languages).

Take a look at this Apache Generated Directory Listing...
https://antofthy.gitlab.io/info/ascii/

This page was generated by Apache. If I add a file, it automatically gets listed, unless I specifically tell it otherwise. In fact 2 files in the directory are removed from the listing as I specifically reference them in the header for the listing. I even used as custom "DefaultIcon" to set the listing icon!

This directory list style was even created more than 30 years ago, AND STILL WORKS!

Actually the web server serving this on isn't even Apache any more but a static web server (gitlab.io)
But I use a local Apache Web Server to re-generate the directly listing, to creates a static "index.html" as part of the upload process. That is if I add a file, and upload it, a new index page is generated showing the new file, auto-magically. It is still Apache Generated though.

As for your problem... You do not need any re-write rules to use index.php as the index file. Just set it as the Directory Index file, and it will be used (if Apcahe has the PHP module, which it must have if you are redirecting to use it!)

Q: How to systematise a checking of "a quite equals to b" (either with round method or | a - b | ~ 0) for any value of a? A:

There's actually a lot more subtlety here than you might expect.

Things that I require from a closeTo style function include:

  1. works sensibly with zero.
  2. works sensibly with very large numbers.
  3. Works sensibly for +/- Infinity and NaN.
  4. if a is close to b, then b is close to a.

Many of the simple solutions only hit 2 or 3 of these. For example, the ratio test above fails 1 and 4, and I'm not sure about 3.

There are two approaches I like:

  1. Treat the doubles as ints and compare as ints. (Not convert the value to an int, but actually treat the underlying bit representation as ints). There are a bunch of tricky edge-cases with this around NaNs, Infinity and negative numbers - but the guts of the idea is that the bit-pattern of positive doubles can be reinterpreted as positive integers, and that maintains ordering and the notion of "nearness". I.e if a has an int representation of 12000 and b has an int representation of 12005 you know there are exactly 4 double values between them and so they are "pretty close". This is a good technique if you want very high accuracy guarantees.

  2. Calculate an allowed delta based on the max-value of |a| and |b|, and clip that to some minimum. i.e. d = max(eps1 * max(|a|,|b|), eps2); return |a-b| < d. If you make the common mistake of basing your d off just one of |a| or |b| you fail case 4 above. (Another common choice is using addition rather than max, d = eps1 * (|a| + |b|) + eps2. This approach is basically allowing a maximum symmetric relative error for large values, and a max absolute error for small values. This tends to be the right choice when your bounds are looser and physically based. You usually need to think about handling NaNs and infinities in a way that matches what you want - this is use-case specific.
